units.title: Describing Motion
units.blurb: Measure in SI units, then describe motion with speed, velocity, acceleration and graphs.

units.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
units.blurb: Forces are pushes and pulls between objects; Newton's three laws say how they change motion, and pressure spreads a force over an area.

units.title: Energy, Work and Heat
units.blurb: Energy takes many forms and is never used up; work, machines and heat move it from place to place.

units.title: Waves, Sound and Light
units.blurb: Waves carry energy without carrying matter along; sound and light are both waves.

units.title: Electricity and Magnetism
units.blurb: Charges push and pull, currents flow around circuits, and currents and magnets are linked.

topics.title: Average Speed
topics.short: Average speed is total distance divided by total time: s = d/t.
topics.trouble: Students average two speeds for a trip instead of dividing the total distance by the total time.

topics.title: Distance-Time Graphs
topics.short: A steeper line means faster; a flat line means stopped.
topics.trouble: Students read the graph as a picture of the path, thinking an uphill line means the object moves uphill.

topics.title: Distance and Displacement
topics.short: Distance is how far you traveled; displacement is how far and which way you ended up from the start.
topics.trouble: Students give the total distance walked when the question asks how far from the start you ended up.

topics.title: Velocity: Speed with a Direction
topics.short: Velocity tells how fast and which way, so turning around changes it even at the same speed.
topics.trouble: Students think two cars going 50 km/h in opposite directions have the same velocity.

topics.title: Acceleration
topics.short: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes: a = Δv/Δt, in meters per second per second.
topics.trouble: Students think acceleration means moving fast, or that slowing down and turning are not acceleration.

topics.title: Speed-Time Graphs
topics.short: On a speed-time graph a rising line means speeding up and a flat line means steady speed.
topics.trouble: Students confuse a flat speed-time line (moving steadily) with a flat distance-time line (stopped).

topics.title: What a Force Is
topics.short: A force is a push or pull between two objects, measured in newtons.
topics.trouble: Students think a force is something a moving object carries inside it, like "the force of the ball", rather than a push between two objects.

topics.title: Net Force and Balanced Forces
topics.short: Add forces along a line, counting direction, to find the net force.
topics.trouble: Students add the sizes of two opposing forces instead of subtracting one from the other.

topics.title: Newton's First Law: Inertia
topics.short: With zero net force, an object keeps the velocity it has, whether still or moving.
topics.trouble: Students believe a moving object needs a force to keep it moving and stops when that force "runs out".

topics.title: Newton's Second Law: F = ma
topics.short: Net force equals mass times acceleration, so the same push speeds up a heavy cart less.
topics.trouble: Students think a steady force gives a steady speed, rather than a steady acceleration.

topics.title: Mass and Weight
topics.short: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the pull of gravity on it: W = mg, with g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth.
topics.trouble: Students think an astronaut's mass changes on the Moon, or give weight in kilograms.

topics.title: Friction
topics.short: Friction acts where surfaces touch, against their sliding, and grows when they press together harder.
topics.trouble: Students think friction only ever slows things down, yet friction on your shoes is what pushes you forward when you walk.

topics.title: Newton's Third Law
topics.short: Forces come in pairs: when A pushes B, B pushes A just as hard in the opposite direction.
topics.trouble: Students think the bigger or faster object pushes harder in a collision.

topics.title: Momentum
topics.short: Momentum is mass times velocity, and in a collision the total momentum stays the same.
topics.trouble: Students think a heavy, slow object always has more momentum than a light, fast one.

topics.title: Softening a Collision
topics.short: Stretching a collision over more time lowers the force, which is how airbags, helmets and crumple zones work.
topics.trouble: Students think padding reduces the change in momentum, when it really spreads the same change over more time.

topics.title: Gravity: Mass and Distance
topics.short: Every two masses attract; more mass means more pull, and twice the distance means a quarter of the pull.
topics.trouble: Students think there is no gravity in space because astronauts float, or that gravity needs air to work.

topics.title: Pressure
topics.short: Pressure is force spread over an area: P = F/A, in pascals (newtons per square meter).
topics.trouble: Students think a bigger force always means more pressure, missing that a wider area spreads it out, as with snowshoes.

topics.title: Forms of Energy
topics.short: Energy shows up as motion, height, stretch, heat, light, sound, chemical and electric energy.
topics.trouble: Students think energy is a substance that gets used up, or mix up energy with force.

topics.title: Kinetic Energy
topics.short: KE = ½mv², so doubling the speed gives four times the energy.
topics.trouble: Students think doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy.

topics.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
topics.short: Lifting an object stores energy: PE = mgh, measured from a chosen level.
topics.trouble: Students switch reference levels partway through a problem, measuring one height from the floor and another from the table.

topics.title: Energy Changes Form
topics.short: As an object falls or swings, energy moves between kinetic and potential, and the total stays the same.
topics.trouble: Students think energy is lost when a swing slows down, rather than turned into heat and sound.

topics.title: Work
topics.short: Work is force times the distance moved along the force: W = Fd, in joules.
topics.trouble: Students think holding a heavy box still is work in the physics sense.

topics.title: Power
topics.short: Power is how fast energy is transferred: P = W/t, in watts.
topics.trouble: Students use watts and joules as if they meant the same thing.

topics.title: Efficiency
topics.short: Efficiency is useful energy out divided by energy in, and it is always less than 100%.
topics.trouble: Students believe a well-built machine can put out more energy than it takes in.

topics.title: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage
topics.short: Ramps, levers and pulleys trade a smaller force for a longer distance.
topics.trouble: Students think a machine reduces the work needed, not just the force.

topics.title: Levers and Balance
topics.short: A lever balances when force times distance from the pivot is the same on both sides.
topics.trouble: Students think the heavier side of a seesaw always goes down, whatever the distances from the pivot.

topics.title: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
topics.short: Heat moves by contact, by moving fluids and by light, including infrared you can't see.
topics.trouble: Students think a metal bench feels colder because it is colder than a wooden one, rather than because it carries heat away faster.

topics.title: Changes of State
topics.short: Melting and boiling take in energy without raising the temperature; freezing and condensing give it back.
topics.trouble: Students think the temperature keeps rising while ice melts or water boils.

topics.title: Parts of a Wave
topics.short: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period describe a wave; the period is 1 divided by the frequency.
topics.trouble: Students think a wave carries the water or rope along with it, rather than carrying energy.

topics.title: The Wave Equation v = fλ
topics.short: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
topics.trouble: Students think a higher frequency makes a wave travel faster, when the medium sets the speed and the wavelength shrinks instead.

topics.title: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
topics.short: In a transverse wave the medium moves across the wave's path; in a longitudinal wave it moves back and forth along it.
topics.trouble: Students think every wave is transverse, like a water wave, and can't picture sound as squeezes and stretches of the air.

topics.title: Sound: Pitch and Loudness
topics.short: Pitch comes from frequency and loudness from amplitude, and sound needs a medium to travel.
topics.trouble: Students link pitch to loudness, thinking louder sounds are higher.

topics.title: Echoes and Sonar
topics.short: Time an echo to find a distance: d = vt/2, because the sound goes there and back.
topics.trouble: Students forget the sound travels there and back, so their answer is twice the real distance.

topics.title: Reflection, Absorption and Transmission
topics.short: When a wave meets a new material it can bounce off, be absorbed or pass through.
topics.trouble: Students think light only reflects from shiny surfaces, not from paper or skin.

topics.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
topics.short: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all light, with different wavelengths.
topics.trouble: Students think radio waves are a kind of sound, or that only visible light is light.

topics.title: Light and Color
topics.short: White light holds all colors, and objects look colored by the light they reflect.
topics.trouble: Students think a red filter adds red to light, rather than blocking the other colors.

topics.title: Refraction and Lenses
topics.short: Light bends when it changes speed at a boundary at an angle, and lenses use this to focus.
topics.trouble: Students expect light to bend even when it meets a boundary straight on.

topics.title: Higher Frequency, More Energy
topics.short: Light comes in tiny packets whose energy rises with frequency, so one ultraviolet or X-ray packet can break molecules in cells and one radio packet can't.
topics.trouble: Students think brighter light means more energetic packets, so they expect bright red light to cause sunburn sooner than dim ultraviolet light.

topics.title: Analog and Digital Signals
topics.short: A digital signal sends information as separate values (0s and 1s), which can still be read exactly after some noise is added.
topics.trouble: Students think "digital" just means electronic, rather than sent as distinct values.

topics.title: Electric Charge
topics.short: Protons are positive and electrons negative; objects become charged by gaining or losing electrons, while the protons stay put.
topics.trouble: Students think an object becomes positive by gaining protons, when it really loses electrons.

topics.title: Attraction and Repulsion
topics.short: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, more strongly when they are closer.
topics.trouble: Students think a charged balloon can't attract a neutral wall, since only opposite charges attract.

topics.title: Fields: Forces at a Distance
topics.short: Gravity, electric and magnetic forces act across space through fields around objects.
topics.trouble: Students think field lines are real strings, or the paths objects must follow.

topics.title: Current and Voltage
topics.short: Current is the flow of charge, in amperes; voltage is the push given to each charge, in volts.
topics.trouble: Students think current gets used up as it passes through a bulb.

topics.title: Complete Circuits
topics.short: Charge flows only around a closed loop, and a switch opens or closes the loop.
topics.trouble: Students connect a bulb to only one end of a battery and expect it to light.

topics.title: Ohm's Law
topics.short: Voltage equals current times resistance: V = IR.
topics.trouble: Students think a resistor's resistance changes when the current through it changes.

topics.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
topics.short: In series one current flows through everything; in parallel each branch gets the full voltage.
topics.trouble: Students think the first bulb in a series circuit is brightest because it gets the current first.

topics.title: Electric Power and Energy Use
topics.short: P = VI, and the energy used is power times time, often in kilowatt-hours.
topics.trouble: Students mix up kilowatts (a rate) with kilowatt-hours (an amount of energy).

topics.title: Magnets and Magnetic Fields
topics.short: Every magnet has a north and a south pole, and its field lines run from north to south outside it.
topics.trouble: Students think breaking a magnet in half separates its north pole from its south pole.

topics.title: Electromagnets and Motors
topics.short: An electric current makes a magnetic field; a coil around iron makes it much stronger.
topics.trouble: Students think only permanent magnets make magnetic fields, not currents.

topics.title: Generators and Induction
topics.short: Moving a magnet near a coil makes a current, so generators turn motion into electricity.
topics.trouble: Students think a magnet resting inside a coil makes a steady current.
